title: FedReview: Review and Dispose Poisoned Updates Without Validation Datasets or Historic Knowledge
KeTS: Kernel-Based Trust Segmentation Against Model Poisoning Attacks
Byzantine-resilient federated edge intrusion detection for heterogeneous IoT networks under non-IID conditions
abstract: Intrusion detection at the edge of the Internet of Things (IoT) runs into two problems at the same time. Traffic is not identically distributed across devices, because a camera, a thermostat and a gateway do not behave alike, and some of the participating nodes cannot be trusted to report honestly. Federated learning fits the setting well, since it keeps raw traffic on the device and shares only model updates. The catch is that its standard averaging rule is fragile. A small group of malicious clients can quietly steer the shared model, and that fragility gets worse once the data is heterogeneous. We study how to keep a federated intrusion detection system accurate when both problems are present at once. We build a compact CNN–BiLSTM detector that is small enough to run on constrained edge hardware, train it federally across twenty non-IID clients, and compare five aggregation rules under three poisoning strategies. The comparison spans 641 completed training runs: five random seeds per configuration for the headline grid and three for the sweep and privacy tiers, with experimental performance results reported as means with 95% confidence intervals and every claim of superiority tested by a paired t-test with Holm correction. On CICIoT2023 every rule reaches an attack-free F1 of 0.989–0.990, and a thirty-percent sign-flipping adversary collapses plain federated averaging to a constant prediction, taking its Matthews correlation from 0.979 to 0.000, while trust-weighted aggregation (FLTrust) and multi-Krum hold 0.981 and 0.980. Sweeping the adversarial fraction from 0.05 to 0.45 locates each rule’s empirical breakdown point: federated averaging fails at 0.05, the coordinate-wise rules at 0.20, and multi-Krum at 0.45, which is exactly the $$(K-2)/2K$$ bound its theory predicts. On the harder TON_IoT and Edge-IIoTset benchmarks no rule is uniformly best: unattacked federated averaging is the strongest configuration, so robustness is insurance carrying a measurable clean-data premium rather than a free improvement. A formal Rényi accounting of the client-level differentially private variant reverses a claim made in the original submission: with twenty clients and full participation there is no privacy amplification by subsampling, and no operating point we evaluated maintains useful detection at a meaningful budget, which we explain with a closed-form noise-to-signal argument rather than leave as an empirical curiosity. Finally, the detector was compiled and timed on a physical ESP32, where one inference takes 23.5 ms using 24.7 KB of flash for weights and 5.0 KB of scratch RAM, reproducing the host logits to within $$6\times 10^{-8}$$ . We release the full training and evaluation pipeline, including a checkpoint-and-resume mechanism, so the comparison can be reproduced.

title: FedShield: Configurable Mean–Median Robust Aggregation for Poisoning-Resilient Federated Healthcare-IoT Learning
abstract: Federated learning lets healthcare-IoT and Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) systems train shared models without centralizing sensitive records, but poisoned client updates can degrade the global model, and the Byzantine-robust aggregators meant to prevent this behave unevenly across the non-IID data partitions these deployments produce. This paper presents FedShield, a configurable robust aggregation rule that ranks client updates with a Krum-style score and combines a narrow top-2 mean with a broader top-7 coordinate-wise median through a single mixing weight fixed per deployment. FedShield is evaluated on four public healthcare-IoT benchmarks—MIT-BIH, PTB-XL, PhysioNet/CinC 2017, and CIC-IoMT-2024—against seven published baselines (FedAvg, Krum, Multi-Krum, Trimmed-Mean, RFA, DnC, and FLTrust) under eight poisoning attacks, four malicious-client ratios, and five seeds. The design target is cross-setting consistency rather than per-cell dominance, and FedShield meets it as the only method that stays in the top three across all twelve dataset–metric cells. Its clearest gains are on the class-concentrated CIC-IoMT-2024 partition, where it lowers the attack-effect rate from 51.5% for the strongest baseline to 12.3%, while PTB-XL is a documented exception on which broad averaging remains preferable. Two adaptive stress tests locate the boundary of this behavior: under centroid-near mimicry and an adaptive Krum-survival attack, malicious updates evade the distance-based filter and plain averaging becomes the stronger response, scoping the result to the evaluated non-adaptive attacks.

title: Federated Art Chase: Privacy Leakage and Data Poisoning in Federated Fine-Tuning
abstract: Federated learning (FL) is increasingly used to adapt a pretrained, centrally fine-tuned model to data that remain on user devices, beyond training a model from scratch. In this report, prepared for the 4th Federated Machine Learning International Summer School, we study the privacy and integrity of this approach with a reproducible pipeline. An ImageNet-pretrained MobileNetV4-Conv-Small model is fine-tuned centrally on ten Quick, Draw! classes (97.50% test accuracy) and then adapted with head-only FedAvg over ten non-IID clients, which raises client training accuracy from 90.34% to 91.49% while preserving global accuracy. We evaluate four adversarial scenarios. First, from a single one-step client update, an honest-but-curious server recovers the complete private label set, but its reconstructions follow class prototypes rather than the private drawings (mean SSIM 0.130). Second, from a one-round FedAvg aggregate, label-count recovery falls from 87.5% with one client to 75.0% with five and ten clients, below the 80.0% of an uninformed uniform guess. Third, under FedAvg, a backdoor injected by 30%, 50%, and 100% of the clients reaches an attack success rate (ASR) of 21.9%, 31.3%, and 54.7% at a cost of at most 0.8 percentage points of clean accuracy, whereas label flipping is effective only when most of the source-class data are relabeled. Fourth, FLTrust with a root set retained from centralized fine-tuning lowers the backdoor ASR to 1.8% and 4.0% at 30% and 50% malicious clients and the label-flipping ASR from 12.6% to 0.8% without measurable clean-accuracy loss, but provides no protection when every client is malicious. The report closes with a live session in which participants draw, fine-tune, and poison the model through Indigma's FedMaestro orchestrator. Code and executed notebooks, runnable on Google Colab, are at https://github.com/Indigma-Innovations/fl-summer-school.

title: Code and results for "Semantic Knowledge-Base Poisoning in AI-Native 6G: A Provenance-Based Meaning-Drift Audit for Trustworthy Federated Semantic Communication"
abstract: This record contains the complete, self-contained code and precomputed results accompanying the article "Semantic Knowledge-Base Poisoning in AI-Native 6G: A Provenance-Based Meaning-Drift Audit for Trustworthy Federated Semantic Communication." It reproduces every table and figure in the paper. The study introduces semantic knowledge-base (KB) poisoning, a targeted attack on federated semantic communication in which a small set of malicious clients steer the recovered meaning of a chosen concept toward an attacker-selected concept while deliberately preserving classification accuracy, rendering the attack largely undetectable by accuracy monitoring. To detect and mitigate it, the framework anchors per-client semantic fingerprints of codebook contributions in a hash-chained ledger, producing a tamper-evident meaning-space drift audit; a simple threshold on this audit is shown to be the strongest, most robust defense. The software (package "s6g") is a reproducible testbed written in pure NumPy, with matplotlib for figures and scikit-learn for the real-modality dataset. It requires no GPU, no deep-learning framework, and no external downloads, and runs end to end on a single CPU in minutes; the transceiver's manual backpropagation is finite-difference verified. Included: the s6g package (synthetic and real semantic spaces, wireless channel, transceiver, attacks, aggregation and detection defenses, provenance ledger and drift audit, and a reinforcement-learning trust policy); experiment drivers for multi-seed statistics, real-modality validation on handwritten digits, an audit-aware adaptive adversary, and detection-based baselines (FLTrust, FoolsGold); raw per-seed results as JSON; generated figures; and a Word README documenting layout, commands, and results. Contents: README.docx, requirements.txt, the s6g/ package, four experiment driver scripts, results/ and figures/ directories, and *_results.json data files. To reproduce, install the requirements and run the drivers as documented in the README; each driver's "report" command prints the aggregated results. Keywords: 6G; semantic communication; federated learning; data poisoning; blockchain provenance; trust; Byzantine robustness.

title: When Does Trust Help? A Leakage-Free Evaluation of Representation- and Aggregation-Based Defenses Against Backdoors in Federated Intrusion Detection
abstract: Federated learning (FL) lets distributed intrusion-detection systems (IDS) train on private traffic, but exposes the global model to poisoning and backdoor attacks under non-IID client data. A popular defense family scores or filters clients using a small trusted "root" dataset and the similarity of client behaviour to a trusted reference. I re-examine these trust-based defenses under a protocol designed to remove common evaluation artifacts: train-only feature standardization, a server root set disjoint from client data, multi-seed (n=6) runs with paired significance tests, formal (varepsilon, delta) accounting for DP-SGD, and a defense-aware adaptive attacker. Across three NIDS datasets (CSE-CIC-IDS2018, NF-ToN-IoT, NF-UNSW-NB15-v2) I find: (1) a representation-similarity aggregator (RepGuard) significantly improves classification utility and seed-stability over FLTrust under heavy non-IID poisoning, and - under severe heterogeneity or many adversaries - also lowers backdoor ASR substantially (e.g., 0.48 vs FLTrust 0.86 at Dirichlet alpha=0.1); (2) at strong trigger magnitudes no defense reduces backdoor attack success rate (ASR approx 0.95); (3) a controlled trigger-magnitude sweep shows defenses help only for small triggers (ASR 0.10 for RepGuard at magnitude 0.5, vs. 0.40 undefended) and collapse to ASR approx 1.0 by magnitude 2; (4) a triggered-canary check that assumes knowledge of the attacker's trigger - the assumption behind much prior "success" - lowers ASR from 0.49 to 0.12, i.e., trigger knowledge, not representation scoring, suppresses the backdoor; (5) correctly-accounted DP-SGD (varepsilon in [0.3, 16]) costs little utility but does not mitigate the backdoor. I release the protocol so future FL-IDS defenses can be evaluated without the leakage and oracle assumptions that inflate reported robustness.

title: A Simulation Study on the Theoretical Potential of Quantum-Enhanced Federated Security Operations
abstract: This paper makes two distinct contributions to the security and federated learning communities. First, we identify and empirically demonstrate a critical vulnerability in Krum, a widely deployed Byzantine-resilient aggregation algorithm, showing catastrophic failure (44.7% accuracy degradation) when applied to high-dimensional neural networks. We provide comprehensive analysis of five alternative algorithms and validate FLTrust as a more resilient solution, though requiring trusted infrastructure. This finding has immediate implications for production federated learning systems. Second, we present a rigorous feasibility analysis of quantum-enhanced security operations through simulation-based exploration. We document fundamental deployment barriers including (1) environmental electromagnetic interference exceeding sensor capabilities by 6-9 orders of magnitude, (2) infrastructure costs of USD 3-5M with unproven benefits, (3) an absence of validated correlation mechanisms between quantum measurements and cyber threats, and (4) O(n2) scalability constraints limiting deployments to 20 nodes. This is purely theoretical research using simulated data without physical quantum sensors. Physical validation through empirical noise characterization and sensor deployment in operational environments represents the critical next step, though faces significant challenges from EMI shielding requirements and calibration procedures. Together, these contributions provide actionable insights for current federated learning deployments while preventing premature investment in quantum sensing for cybersecurity.
